verse.text: Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, and Timothy our brother, to the assembly of God that is in Corinth, together with all the holy ones who are in the whole of Achaia:
verse.note: The Greek word was the ordinary term for a civic gathering and the Septuagint’s word for Israel assembled before God. “Church” is the near-universal rendering and readers know what it refers to, but it now suggests a building or an institution. “Assembly” is used throughout this translation so that the reader sees one word wherever the Greek has one.

The word is used of all members of the community as people set apart for God, echoing the Septuagint’s language for Israel. “Saints” is the traditional rendering and many translations keep it, but it now suggests canonized individuals or people of exceptional virtue. Other versions use “God’s people” or “his holy people.”

verse.text: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and God of all comfort,
verse.note: The noun and its verb occur ten times in verses 3–7, and the repetition is kept in English. The Greek word covers both consoling and strengthening, so “encouragement” is also possible. It echoes the Septuagint’s language for God comforting his people, as in Isaiah 40:1.

verse.text: who comforts us in all our affliction, so that we can comfort those in any affliction with the comfort with which we ourselves are comforted by God.
For just as the sufferings of Christ overflow to us, so through Christ our comfort overflows as well.
If we are afflicted, it is for your comfort and salvation; if we are comforted, it is for your comfort, which takes effect as you endure the same sufferings that we also suffer.
And our hope for you is firm, because we know that as you share in the sufferings, so you share also in the comfort.
For we do not want you to be unaware, brothers and sisters, of the affliction that came upon us in Asia: we were weighed down so excessively, beyond our strength, that we despaired even of living.
verse.note: The Greek plural was the normal way to address a mixed group of men and women, and Paul is writing to the whole community. “Brothers” alone now sounds as though only men are addressed. Many recent translations make the same choice; others keep “brothers” with a footnote.

verse.text: Indeed, we ourselves had the sentence of death within us, so that we would trust not in ourselves but in God, who raises the dead.
He rescued us from so great a death, and he will rescue us; on him we have set our hope that he will rescue us yet again,
verse.note: Some manuscripts read a present tense here (“and does rescue”), which lies behind the King James Version’s past, present and future sequence. The earliest witnesses have the future, and a few omit the phrase altogether. The future is the reading most editors prefer, even though it repeats the following clause.

verse.text: as you too join in helping by praying for us, so that many people may give thanks on our behalf for the gift granted to us through many.

note.traditional: by the means of many persons

verse.note: The Greek sentence is compressed and can be construed in more than one way. Here “through many” is taken with the gift, meaning that God’s rescue came in answer to the prayers of many. It could instead go with the thanksgiving (“thanks may be given by many”), and the phrase rendered “many people” is literally “many faces,” perhaps picturing faces turned up in prayer.

verse.text: For this is our boast, the testimony of our conscience: that we have conducted ourselves in the world, and all the more toward you, with the holiness and sincerity that come from God, not by fleshly wisdom but by the grace of God.
verse.note: Manuscripts are divided between “holiness” and a similar-looking Greek word meaning “simplicity” or “frankness.” The latter suits the context of Paul defending his straightforwardness and is preferred by some editors and translations. The Greek text translated here reads “holiness,” which has strong early support.

In Paul’s usage “flesh” often stands for human nature left to its own resources, apart from God, and not specifically for the body or its appetites. “Fleshly wisdom” is therefore merely human shrewdness, and “according to the flesh” in verse 17 means planning by self-interested human calculation. Some translations paraphrase as “worldly” or “earthly” wisdom.

verse.text: For we write you nothing other than what you read and indeed understand, and I hope that you will understand fully,
verse.note: The Greek phrase can mean “to the end” (in time, until the day of the Lord mentioned in verse 14) or “completely.” The contrast with “in part” in the next verse favors “fully,” but both readings are well supported. The sentence also plays on two similar Greek verbs, “read” and “understand,” which English cannot reproduce.

verse.text: just as you have also understood us in part—that we are your boast, just as you are ours, on the day of our Lord Jesus.
In this confidence I intended to come to you first, so that you might have a second favor,
verse.note: The word is the one usually rendered “grace”; here it refers to the benefit the Corinthians would receive from a second visit, though some take it as a second occasion of divine grace. A number of manuscripts read a similar word meaning “joy.” Paul’s plan was to visit Corinth both on the way to Macedonia and on the way back.

verse.text: and to go on through you to Macedonia, and from Macedonia to come back to you and be sent on my way by you to Judea.
So when I intended this, was I being fickle? Or do I make my plans according to the flesh, so that with me it is both “Yes, yes” and “No, no”?
But as God is faithful, our word to you is not “Yes and No.”
For the Son of God, Jesus Christ, who was proclaimed among you by us—by me and Silvanus and Timothy—was not “Yes and No”; rather, in him it has been “Yes.”
For however many God’s promises are, in him is the “Yes.” That is why it is also through him that the “Amen” is spoken by us to God for his glory.
Now it is God who makes us firm with you in Christ and who anointed us,
verse.note: There is a wordplay in the Greek: “Christ” (Christos) means “anointed one,” and the verb “anointed” (chrisas) follows immediately. The terms in verses 21–22 for making firm, sealing and giving a down payment were also used in commerce for guaranteeing a transaction, so Paul describes God as standing surety for his people.

verse.text: who also sealed us and gave us the Spirit in our hearts as a down payment.
verse.note: The word is a commercial term for a first installment that secures a transaction and obliges the payer to complete it. “Earnest” is no longer understood in this sense, and “guarantee” loses the idea that part of the payment has already been made. The Spirit is itself the down payment: the Greek is literally “the down payment of the Spirit.”

verse.text: But I call on God as my witness, on my life, that it was to spare you that I did not come again to Corinth.
verse.note: Paul swears an oath, inviting God to act against him if he is lying. The Greek word traditionally rendered “soul” here means his life or his very self, which is what he stakes on the truth of his statement. Several modern versions paraphrase as “against me.”

verse.text: Not that we lord it over your faith; rather, we are coworkers for your joy, for it is by faith that you stand.
For I made up my mind about this: that I would not come to you again in grief.
verse.note: Paul appears to refer to an earlier visit to Corinth that went badly, usually called the “painful visit,” made between 1 Corinthians and this letter; Acts does not record it. The Greek noun and its verb occur eight times in verses 1–7 and are rendered “grief” and “grieve” throughout so that the repetition can be heard. Other translations use “pain” or “sorrow.”

verse.text: For if I grieve you, then who is there to make me glad except the one who is grieved by me?
And I wrote this very thing so that when I came I would not have grief from those who ought to have made me rejoice, being confident about all of you that my joy is the joy of you all.
verse.note: Paul refers to an earlier letter written in tears (verse 4; see also 7:8–12). Most scholars think it is a lost letter sent after the painful visit; older interpreters identified it with 1 Corinthians, and some propose that part of it survives in chapters 10–13. The Greek can also be read “I wrote for this very reason.”

verse.text: For out of great distress and anguish of heart I wrote to you through many tears, not so that you would be grieved, but so that you would know the love I have so abundantly for you.
verse.note: The Greek word is usually rendered “affliction” or “tribulation” and normally refers to hardship pressing on someone from outside. Here it is paired with “anguish of heart” and describes Paul’s inner state as he wrote, so “distress” is used. Several modern translations do the same.

verse.text: But if anyone has caused grief, it is not me he has grieved but, to some extent—not to overstate it—all of you.
verse.note: Paul does not name the person. Older interpreters identified him with the man living with his father’s wife in 1 Corinthians 5; most scholars now think he was someone who openly opposed or insulted Paul during the painful visit. Neither identification can be proved.

The verb means “to weigh down” or “to burden,” and the sentence is compressed. Most interpreters take it as a parenthesis in which Paul avoids pressing the charge too heavily: the offender has grieved the whole congregation, at least to some degree. An older reading punctuates differently: “he has grieved me only in part—so that I do not burden you all.”

verse.text: This punishment by the majority is sufficient for such a person,
so that, on the contrary, you should rather forgive and comfort him, or such a person may be swallowed up by his excessive grief.
So I urge you to confirm your love for him.
verse.note: The verb was used for formally ratifying a decision, a will or an agreement (compare Galatians 3:15). Paul may be asking for a public act by the congregation that reverses the punishment, not only a change of feeling. Many translations have “reaffirm.”

verse.text: For this is also why I wrote: to find out how you stand the test, whether you are obedient in everything.
Anyone you forgive anything, I forgive too. For indeed what I have forgiven—if I have forgiven anything—I have forgiven for your sake in the presence of Christ,
verse.note: Literally “in the face of Christ.” Most interpreters take this to mean that Paul forgives with Christ looking on, as his witness. The King James Version’s “in the person of Christ” understands it as acting as Christ’s representative, which is possible but less likely for this idiom.

verse.text: so that we are not taken advantage of by Satan; for we are not ignorant of his designs.
Now when I came to Troas for the good news of Christ, and a door had been opened for me in the Lord,
verse.note: “Gospel” is now a religious term or the name of a book. The Greek was an ordinary word for an announcement of good news, used also of public and imperial proclamations. Many modern translations alternate between “good news” and “gospel.”

verse.text: I had no relief for my spirit, because I did not find my brother Titus there; instead I took leave of them and went on to Macedonia.
But thanks be to God, who always leads us in triumphal procession in Christ and through us reveals the scent of the knowledge of him in every place.
verse.note: A Roman triumph was the parade of a victorious general through the city, with captives displayed before the crowds. In usage of the period this verb with a personal object normally means to lead someone as a conquered captive in such a parade, which would make Paul God’s prisoner on display. Whether Paul intends that sense or pictures himself as sharing in the victory is debated. The older rendering “causes us to triumph” has little support in Greek usage.

verse.text: For we are the fragrance of Christ to God among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing:
verse.note: In the Septuagint the word rendered “fragrance” regularly describes the pleasing smell of a sacrifice rising to God, often paired with the word rendered “scent” in verses 14 and 16. Many interpreters also think of the incense burned along the route of a triumphal procession, continuing the image of verse 14. Both associations may be in play.

verse.text: to the one a scent from death to death, to the other a scent from life to life. And who is sufficient for these things?
verse.note: The earliest manuscripts read “from death to death” and “from life to life.” Many later manuscripts lack the word “from,” giving “a scent of death to death” and “of life to life,” which is the reading behind the King James Version.

verse.text: For we are not, like so many, peddling the word of God; rather, we speak out of sincerity, as from God, in the sight of God, in Christ.
verse.note: The verb comes from the world of the petty retailer or tavern keeper, a trade with a reputation for cheating, especially by watering down wine. It suggests both selling for profit and tampering with the goods, which is why older versions have “corrupt.” The same image was used in Greek writers against teachers who sold their wisdom.

verse.text: Are we beginning to commend ourselves again? Or do we, like some, need letters of commendation to you or from you?
verse.note: Travelers in the ancient world commonly carried letters of introduction from a known person vouching for them to a host or community. Paul's rivals at Corinth apparently arrived with such letters. The rendering “commendation” keeps the Greek link with “commend ourselves” in the same verse.

verse.text: You yourselves are our letter, written on our hearts, known and read by all people.
verse.note: A few manuscripts read “your hearts,” and some translations follow them. The great majority of witnesses read “our hearts,” which is the text translated here. The two Greek words differ by a single letter and were pronounced alike.

verse.text: You show plainly that you are a letter from Christ, delivered by us, written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone but on tablets that are hearts of flesh.
Such is the confidence we have through Christ toward God.
Not that we are competent of ourselves to reckon anything as coming from ourselves; rather, our competence is from God,
who has also made us competent to be servants of a new covenant, not of the letter but of the Spirit; for the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.
verse.note: This is a different Greek word from the “letter” (epistle) of verses 1–3. It means a written character or a written text, and here refers to the law as something written, as verse 7 makes explicit with “letters on stones.” The contrast is between a covenant inscribed externally and one in which God's Spirit works within, echoing Jeremiah 31 and Ezekiel 36.

verse.text: Now if the service of death, engraved in letters on stones, came in glory, so that the children of Israel could not gaze at the face of Moses because of the glory of his face, a glory that was being set aside,
verse.note: Most translations have “ministry” (older ones “ministration”) here and “ministers” in verse 6. The Greek words were everyday terms for carrying out a task on someone's behalf and did not denote a religious office. “Service” and “servants” keep that ordinary sense and show that the two words are related.

Many modern translations speak of a “fading” glory here and in verses 11 and 13. Elsewhere the verb means to put out of operation or bring to an end, not to grow dim, and Exodus 34 says nothing of the radiance fading. Some scholars defend “fading” as a sense suggested by the context; others reject it as lacking support in Greek usage. The same rendering is kept all four times the verb occurs in this chapter.

verse.text: how will the service of the Spirit not be in glory all the more?
For if there was glory in the service of condemnation, much more does the service of righteousness abound in glory.
For in fact, what has been glorified has in this respect not been glorified at all, because of the glory that surpasses it.
For if what was being set aside came with glory, what remains is much more in glory.
Since, then, we have such a hope, we act with great openness,
verse.note: The usual rendering is “boldness” or “plainness of speech.” The word meant the freedom to speak without reserve. Here the contrast is with Moses veiling his face, so the point is that nothing is concealed or held back, more than that Paul is courageous.

verse.text: and not like Moses, who used to put a veil over his face so that the children of Israel would not gaze at the end of what was being set aside.
verse.note: The Greek word can mean either the termination of something or its goal and outcome. On the first reading Moses kept Israel from seeing the glory come to its end; on the second, from seeing what the passing arrangement was pointing toward. “End” is kept because English allows both senses.

verse.text: But their minds were hardened. For to this very day the same veil remains at the reading of the old covenant, not lifted, because it is in Christ that it is set aside.
verse.note: This is the only place in the New Testament where the phrase “old covenant” occurs. It refers to the covenant made at Sinai as read aloud from the books of Moses in the synagogue (compare “whenever Moses is read” in verse 15). It is not yet a title for a collection of books, as “Old Testament” later became.

note.term: it is in Christ that it is set aside

verse.note: The Greek can also be read “it not being revealed that in Christ it is set aside,” in which case what is set aside is the old covenant, not the veil. The verb translated “lifted” is the same one rendered “unveiled” in verse 18. Translations and commentators are divided; the rendering here follows the more common reading, in which the veil stays in place because only in Christ is it removed.

verse.text: Indeed, to this day, whenever Moses is read, a veil lies over their hearts;
but whenever someone turns to the Lord, the veil is taken away.
verse.note: The Greek verb has no stated subject. It could be “their heart” from verse 15, Israel, or anyone at all. The wording adapts Exodus 34:34, where Moses removed the veil whenever he went in before the Lord, so Moses is the pattern for whoever turns.

verse.text: Now the Lord is the Spirit, and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom.
verse.note: Many interpreters take this as a comment on the Exodus passage just echoed: “the Lord” to whom one turns in that text corresponds, in present experience, to the Spirit. Others read it as a more direct statement about the risen Christ and the Spirit. The next clause, “the Spirit of the Lord,” shows that Paul still distinguishes the two.

verse.text: And we all, with unveiled face, beholding as in a mirror the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image, from glory to glory, as from the Lord, the Spirit.
verse.note: The verb is formed from the word for “mirror” and in this form normally means to look at something in a mirror. Some translations render it “reflecting,” which would suit the comparison with Moses' shining face, but that sense is poorly attested. Most scholars prefer “beholding,” though the question remains open.

verse.text: For this reason, since we have this service, just as we were shown mercy, we do not lose heart.
verse.note: The Greek word was an everyday term for service or for carrying out a task on someone’s behalf, and did not name a religious office. Most English versions use “ministry” here. That word now suggests a clergy profession, and it hides the link with the related words for “servant” and “serve”.

verse.text: Rather, we have renounced the shameful things that are kept hidden. We do not walk in cunning or tamper with the word of God, but by making the truth visible we commend ourselves to every person’s conscience in the sight of God.
And even if our good news is veiled, it is veiled among those who are perishing.
verse.note: The Greek was an ordinary word for a public announcement of good news. “Gospel” is the traditional rendering, but it is now heard as a religious term or a book title. Many modern translations alternate between the two.

verse.text: In their case the god of this age has blinded the minds of the unbelieving, so that they do not see the light of the good news of the glory of Christ, who is the image of God.
verse.note: The Greek word is a time-word meaning an era, here the present age as opposed to the age to come. Many versions keep “world”, though several recent ones have “age”. Most interpreters take the phrase to refer to Satan. A minority, including some ancient commentators, took it to mean God himself.

note.term: so that they do not see

verse.note: The verb can mean “see clearly” or “shine”. On the second reading the clause would be “so that the light of the good news … does not shine on them”. Most modern translations and lexicons prefer “see” here, but the matter is not settled.

verse.text: For we do not proclaim ourselves, but Christ Jesus as Lord, and ourselves as your slaves for Jesus’ sake.
verse.note: The Greek word is the ordinary term for a slave, a person owned by another. It is not the word for a hired servant. Many English versions soften it to “servants”. The stronger word sharpens Paul’s contrast between proclaiming Jesus as Lord and presenting himself as belonging to the Corinthians.

verse.text: For the God who said, “Light will shine out of darkness,” is the one who has shone in our hearts to bring the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Christ.

note.term: Light will shine out of darkness

verse.note: This is not an exact quotation of any one passage. It recalls God’s first words in creation, “Let there be light” (Genesis 1:3), and perhaps also Isaiah 9:2, where light shines on people in darkness. Paul presents the coming of the knowledge of Christ as an act of the same creator.

verse.text: But we have this treasure in clay jars, so that the surpassing power may be God’s and not from us.
We are afflicted in every way but not crushed, at a loss but not utterly at a loss,

note.term: at a loss but not utterly at a loss

verse.note: The Greek pairs a verb with its own intensified form, a wordplay the traditional rendering loses. The first verb means to be at a loss or without resources. The second adds a prefix meaning “completely”.

verse.text: persecuted but not abandoned, struck down but not destroyed,
always carrying around in the body the dying of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus may also be made visible in our body.
verse.note: Paul does not use the ordinary word for death here, which appears in the next two verses. This rarer noun can mean either the process of being put to death or the resulting state of deadness. “Dying” takes it as the process, which fits the ongoing dangers just listed. Many versions simply have “death”.

verse.text: For we who are alive are constantly being handed over to death for Jesus’ sake, so that the life of Jesus may also be made visible in our mortal flesh.
verse.note: This is the ordinary Greek verb for handing a person into someone else’s power. It is the same verb used throughout the Gospels for Jesus being handed over to the authorities and to death. Rendering it the same way here lets the reader hear that echo.

verse.text: So death is at work in us, but life in you.
But having the same spirit of faith, in keeping with what is written, “I believed, therefore I spoke,” we too believe, and therefore we also speak,
verse.note: “Spirit” may mean a disposition, the same believing attitude as the psalmist’s. It may instead mean the Holy Spirit as the one who produces faith, which would be written “Spirit”. Most translations use the lowercase reading, but a number of scholars defend the reference to God’s Spirit.

The quotation is from Psalm 116:10 in the wording of the ancient Greek translation, where it is numbered Psalm 115:1. The psalm is a thanksgiving by someone rescued from death, which suits Paul’s argument here. The Hebrew of the line is harder and is translated in various ways.

verse.text: knowing that the one who raised Jesus will raise us also with Jesus and will present us together with you.
For all of this is for your sake, so that grace, increasing through an increasing number of people, may make thanksgiving overflow to the glory of God.

note.term: increasing through an increasing number of people

verse.note: The Greek plays on two related words for “more”, and its syntax can be divided in more than one way. “Through the greater number” may go with the grace that increases, as here. It may instead go with the thanksgiving, giving “grace, having increased, may cause thanksgiving to overflow through the many”. The overall sense is the same: more people receiving grace means more thanks to God.

verse.text: Therefore we do not lose heart. Even if our outer self is wasting away, our inner self is being renewed day by day.
For our light, momentary affliction is producing for us an eternal weight of glory that surpasses all measure,
verse.note: Paul sets the “light” affliction against a “weight” of glory. In Hebrew the usual word for glory is related to the word for heaviness, and Paul may be playing on that association. “Eternal” here means belonging to the age to come, in contrast with “this age” in verse 4, as well as unending.

verse.text: as we fix our gaze not on what is seen but on what is not seen. For what is seen is temporary, but what is not seen is eternal.
For we know that if our earthly house, this tent, is taken down, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal, in the heavens.
For indeed in this tent we groan, longing to put on over it our dwelling from heaven,

note.traditional: to be clothed upon; to be further clothed

verse.note: The verb means to put one garment on over another. Paul shifts from the image of a tent to that of clothing: he longs not to be stripped of the present body but to have the heavenly one put on over it. The rendering keeps this “over” sense, which “be clothed” alone loses.

verse.text: if indeed, having put it on, we will not be found naked.
verse.note: Most manuscripts read “having put it on,” which is followed here. A few witnesses read “having taken it off,” giving “even when we have taken it off we will not be found naked”; some modern editions prefer that reading because it avoids an apparent tautology. The two Greek words differ by a single letter.

verse.text: For indeed we who are in this tent groan, weighed down, because we do not want to take it off but to put the other on over it, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life.
Now the one who prepared us for this very thing is God, who gave us the Spirit as a down payment.
verse.note: This was a commercial term for the first installment paid on a purchase, which bound the buyer to pay the rest. Older versions have “earnest” and many modern ones “guarantee” or “deposit.” “Down payment” keeps the point that the Spirit is itself a first part of what is promised, not only an assurance of it.

verse.text: So we are always confident, and we know that while we are at home in the body we are away from the Lord;
for we walk by faith, not by sight.
We are confident, I say, and would rather be away from the body and at home with the Lord.
So we also make it our ambition, whether at home or away, to be pleasing to him.
For we must all stand revealed before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each may be repaid for what was done through the body, according to what each has done, whether good or bad.
verse.note: The verb means to be made visible or shown openly, which is more than turning up in court. Paul uses the same verb twice in the next verse of his own openness to God and to the Corinthians, and the rendering keeps that link. Most translations have “appear” here and “be made manifest” or “be known” in verse 11.

verse.text: Knowing, then, the fear of the Lord, we try to persuade people; but to God we stand revealed, and I hope that we stand revealed in your consciences as well.
We are not commending ourselves to you again but giving you an opportunity to boast about us, so that you may have an answer for those who boast in outward appearance and not in the heart.
For if we were out of our mind, it was for God; if we are in our right mind, it is for you.
verse.note: The verb can describe madness or a state of religious ecstasy. Paul may be answering a charge that he was unbalanced, or referring to visionary experiences that he treats as a matter between himself and God. The Greek does not settle which, and scholars are divided.

verse.text: For the love of Christ holds us in its grip, because we have reached this judgment: one died for all, and so all died.
verse.note: The Greek can mean Christ’s love for us or our love for Christ. Most interpreters take it as Christ’s love, shown in his death described in the next clause. The verb rendered “holds us in its grip” means to hem in or hold fast, and is variously translated “constrains,” “controls” or “compels.”

verse.text: And he died for all so that those who live might no longer live for themselves but for the one who died for them and was raised.
So from now on we know no one according to the flesh. Even if we once knew Christ according to the flesh, we now know him that way no longer.

note.traditional: according to the flesh; from a human point of view

verse.note: “Flesh” in Paul often means human life and its standards apart from God, not the body or sensuality. Most scholars take the phrase here with the verb: it describes a merely human way of assessing people, which Paul once applied even to Christ. A minority connect it with “Christ,” as a reference to knowing Jesus in his earthly life.

verse.text: So if anyone is in Christ, there is a new creation: the old things have passed away; look, new things have come!

note.traditional: he is a new creature; he is a new creation

verse.note: The Greek has no verb: literally, “if anyone in Christ, new creation.” The traditional rendering supplies “he is,” making the person the new creation. The rendering here supplies “there is,” on the view that Paul means the new world God promised has arrived for anyone in Christ. Both are grammatically possible and both have scholarly support.

verse.text: And all of this is from God, who reconciled us to himself through Christ and gave us the service of reconciliation:
verse.note: Most English translations have “ministry of reconciliation.” The Greek word was an everyday term for service or for a task carried out on someone’s behalf, and did not denote a religious office. “Ministry” now suggests clergy or a church profession. “Service” is a recognized lexical gloss and keeps the link with the related words for “servant” and “serve.”

verse.text: that God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself, not counting their offenses against them, and entrusting to us the message of reconciliation.

note.term: God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself
note.traditional: God was in Christ, reconciling the world unto himself; in Christ God was reconciling the world to himself

verse.note: The Greek can be read as a statement that God was in Christ, with the reconciling as a further description, or as “in Christ God was reconciling the world,” where “in Christ” names the means. The rendering follows the Greek word order and leaves both readings open. Many scholars favor the second.

The word means a wrongful act against God or another person. “Trespass,” the traditional rendering, now chiefly suggests entering property without permission. “Offense” is a standard lexical gloss; other versions use “transgressions” or “sins.” The meaning itself is not disputed.

verse.text: So we are ambassadors on Christ’s behalf, with God making his appeal through us. We beg on Christ’s behalf: be reconciled to God.
The one who knew no sin he made to be sin for us, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.
verse.note: Paul’s compressed phrase is usually taken to mean that God treated the sinless Christ as identified with human sin. Some interpreters note that in the Greek Old Testament the same word can mean “sin offering,” and read “made him a sin offering for us.” The rendering keeps Paul’s starker wording, which sets “sin” against “righteousness” in the same sentence.

Greek has one word-family where English has two: righteous and just, righteousness and justice, justify. The phrase can mean a right standing that comes from God or God’s own action in setting things right. Some scholars prefer “justice” or “covenant faithfulness.” The traditional word is kept because “justice of God” would suggest punishment to many modern readers.

verse.text: Working together with him, we also urge you not to receive the grace of God in vain.
verse.note: The Greek says only “working together” and names no partner. Most translations supply “with him” (God), because 5:20 has just said that God makes his appeal through Paul. It could instead mean working together with the Corinthians, or with Paul’s fellow workers.

verse.text: For he says, “At an acceptable time I listened to you, and on a day of salvation I helped you.” Look, now is the truly acceptable time; look, now is the day of salvation!
verse.note: The quotation is Isaiah 49:8 in its Greek form, where God answers his servant at a time of his favor. In his comment Paul replaces the quotation’s word for “acceptable” with a strengthened compound of the same word, which “truly acceptable” tries to keep audible.

verse.text: We give no cause for stumbling in anything, so that our service may not be faulted;
verse.note: The Greek is an everyday word for service or a task carried out for someone, and it is the noun matching “servants” in the next verse. “Ministry,” used by most translations, now suggests a clerical profession, which the word did not denote.

verse.text: rather, as servants of God we commend ourselves in everything: in great endurance, in afflictions, in hardships, in distresses,
in beatings, in imprisonments, in riots, in labors, in sleepless nights, in going without food,
verse.note: The word normally means fasting as a religious practice, and some interpreters take it that way here. In a list of beatings, imprisonments and sleepless nights, most take it as hunger forced on Paul by his work and travels (compare 11:27). The rendering leaves both possible.

verse.text: in purity, in knowledge, in patience, in kindness, in the Holy Spirit, in love without pretense,
verse.note: The phrase has no article and stands in the middle of a list of personal qualities, so some read it as “in a spirit of holiness,” that is, a holy disposition. Most translations take it as the Holy Spirit, which is what the same phrase regularly means elsewhere in Paul.

verse.text: in the word of truth, in the power of God; through the weapons of righteousness for the right hand and the left,
verse.note: This may mean the message Paul proclaims (“the word of truth,” the gospel) or the manner of his speaking (“truthful speech”). Translations are divided, and the Greek allows either.

note.term: the weapons of righteousness for the right hand and the left
note.traditional: the armour of righteousness on the right hand and on the left

verse.note: A soldier carried a weapon of attack, sword or spear, in the right hand and a shield in the left, so the phrase means being fully armed for offense and defense. “Righteousness” belongs to a single Greek word-family that English splits between righteous and just, righteousness and justice. Here the weapons are probably those that righteousness supplies, or that serve it.

verse.text: through honor and dishonor, through ill repute and good repute; as deceivers and yet true,
as unknown and yet well known, as dying and, look, we live, as disciplined and yet not put to death,
as grieving yet always rejoicing, as poor yet making many rich, as having nothing and yet possessing everything.
Our mouth has opened to you, Corinthians; our heart is opened wide.
You are not cramped in us, but you are cramped in your own affections.
As a fair return—I speak as to children—be opened wide yourselves as well.
Do not be yoked in a mismatched team with unbelievers. For what do righteousness and lawlessness have in common, or what fellowship does light have with darkness?
verse.note: The rare verb means to be yoked with an animal of a different kind, and echoes the laws against pairing different animals (Leviticus 19:19; Deuteronomy 22:10). The traditional “unequally” can suggest a difference of rank or strength, where the point is a difference of kind. Paul does not say which associations he means, and interpreters differ over how widely to apply it.

verse.text: What harmony is there between Christ and Beliar, or what share does a believer have with an unbeliever?
verse.note: Beliar is a form of the Hebrew word belial, “worthlessness,” which Jewish writings of the period used as a name for the chief of the evil powers, that is, Satan. This is its only occurrence in the New Testament. Some manuscripts spell it “Belial,” the form familiar from older English Bibles.

verse.text: And what agreement does the sanctuary of God have with idols? For we are the sanctuary of the living God, just as God said: “I will dwell among them and walk among them, and I will be their God, and they will be my people.
verse.note: Greek has one word for the whole temple complex and another, used here, for the building in which the deity dwells. Most translations render both as “temple.” This translation uses “sanctuary” for the second, which keeps Paul’s point that the community is the place where the living God lives.

Many manuscripts read “you are the sanctuary of the living God,” probably under the influence of 1 Corinthians 3:16. The earliest witnesses favor “we are,” and most modern editions and translations follow them.

What follows through verse 18 is a chain of scriptural phrases woven into one statement, drawing on Leviticus 26:11–12 and Ezekiel 37:27, then Isaiah 52:11, Ezekiel 20:34 and 2 Samuel 7:14, with “daughters” perhaps from Isaiah 43:6. The wording follows the Greek version freely. Because 6:14–7:1 breaks into Paul’s appeal for open hearts, some scholars think it was a separate piece placed here, while others defend it as original to the letter.

text.q: Therefore come out from their midst and be separate, says the Lord, and touch nothing unclean; and I will welcome you,
and I will be a father to you, and you will be sons and daughters to me, says the Lord Almighty.”

verse.text: Since we have these promises, then, dear friends, let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of body and spirit, bringing holiness to completion in the fear of God.
verse.note: The promises are the Scripture quotations that close the previous chapter: that God will live among his people, welcome them, and be a Father to them. This verse draws the conclusion of that argument, and the chapter division falls awkwardly in the middle of it.

The Greek word is literally “flesh,” and many versions keep it. Here and in verse 5 Paul uses it in its ordinary sense of the physical person, not in his special sense of human nature opposed to God, so “body” is clearer for a modern reader. Several modern versions do the same.

verse.text: Make room for us. We have wronged no one, ruined no one, taken advantage of no one.
I do not say this to condemn you, for I have already said that you are in our hearts, to die together and to live together.
Great is my frankness toward you; great is my boasting about you. I am filled with comfort; I am overflowing with joy in all our affliction.
verse.note: The word’s basic sense is freedom to speak one’s mind without reserve. Older versions have “boldness of speech,” and some modern ones take it as “confidence” in the Corinthians. In a passage where Paul insists that his heart is open to them and asks them to make room for him, unreserved speech fits best, but the choice is one of nuance and is not settled.

verse.text: For even when we came into Macedonia, our bodies had no relief; instead we were afflicted in every way—conflicts outside, fears inside.
But God, who comforts the downcast, comforted us by the arrival of Titus,
verse.note: The phrase echoes the Greek version of Isaiah 49:13, where God comforts the lowly among his people. The word can mean “humble” or “lowly” in status; here, after the conflicts and fears of verse 5, it describes those brought low by circumstances.

This is the same Greek word used elsewhere for the “coming” of Christ. It was an everyday word for someone’s arrival or presence, and it is rendered “arrival” here because it refers to an ordinary person. Paul had been anxiously waiting for Titus to return from Corinth with news (2:12–13).

verse.text: and not only by his arrival but also by the comfort with which he was comforted over you, as he reported to us your longing, your mourning, your zeal for me, so that I rejoiced still more.
For even if I grieved you with my letter, I do not regret it. Even if I did regret it (I see that that letter did grieve you, though only for a while),
verse.note: This is the letter Paul says he wrote “with many tears” (2:3–4). Older interpreters identified it with 1 Corinthians and the wrongdoer of verse 12 with the man of 1 Corinthians 5. Most scholars now think it was a separate letter, probably lost, written after a painful visit in which someone at Corinth wronged Paul or his representative. The matter remains uncertain.

note.term: Even if I did regret it

verse.note: Paul’s sentence is broken in the Greek, and editors punctuate it differently. Here the clause is taken with “now I rejoice” in verse 9, with the remark about the letter as a parenthesis. Others attach it to what precedes: “I do not regret it, though I did regret it.” Some manuscripts add “for” before “I see,” which smooths the syntax.

verse.text: now I rejoice—not because you were grieved, but because you were grieved into turning back. For you were grieved as God willed, so that you suffered no loss in anything through us.
verse.note: The traditional rendering is “repentance,” which most translations keep as an established term understood to include a change of life. In modern English “repent” centers on feeling sorry, whereas the Greek word carries the prophets’ call to return to God, a change of direction. The difference matters here, because Paul distinguishes the grief from the turning it led to, and uses a separate word for “regret.”

note.traditional: after a godly manner; godly sorrow

verse.note: The Greek phrase is literally “according to God,” and in verse 10 it is set against “the world’s grief.” Most versions have “godly grief” or “godly sorrow.” Since “godly” now suggests merely “pious,” the phrase is rendered by its sense: grief of the kind God intends and approves. Some versions similarly have “as God intended.”

verse.text: For grief as God wills it brings about a turning back that leads to salvation and leaves no regret, but the world’s grief produces death.
verse.note: The Greek adjective “unregretted” could describe either the turning back or the salvation, and interpreters are divided. The rendering leaves it attached to the turning back and its outcome together. The word picks up “regret” from verse 8: Paul does not regret his letter, and the turning back it produced is nothing to regret either.

verse.text: For see how much earnestness this very thing, being grieved as God wills, has produced in you—and more: what a defense of yourselves, what indignation, what fear, what longing, what zeal, what punishment of the wrong! In every way you have shown yourselves to be innocent in the matter.

So then, even though I wrote to you, it was not for the sake of the one who did the wrong, nor for the sake of the one who was wronged, but so that your earnestness for us might be made plain to you before God.
This is why we have been comforted. And on top of our comfort, we rejoiced far more still at the joy of Titus, because his spirit has been refreshed by all of you.
For if I have boasted to him at all about you, I was not put to shame; rather, just as everything we said to you was true, so also our boasting before Titus has proved true.
And his affection for you is all the greater as he remembers the obedience of all of you, how you received him with fear and trembling.
I rejoice that in everything I have confidence in you.
Now we want you to know, brothers and sisters, about the grace of God that has been given among the assemblies of Macedonia:
verse.note: The Greek word was the ordinary term for a civic gathering and the Septuagint’s word for Israel assembled before God. “Church” is the near-universal rendering and readers know what it refers to, but it now suggests a building or an institution. “Assembly” is used throughout this translation so that the one Greek word is always visible.

note.traditional: grace (v. 1, 9); favor or gift (v. 4); gracious work (v. 6, 7, 19); thanks (v. 16)

verse.note: Paul uses one Greek word throughout this chapter for God’s grace (verses 1 and 9), for the privilege of taking part in the collection (verse 4), for the collection itself (verses 6, 7 and 19), and for thanks to God (verse 16). Many translations vary the English to suit each sense. Here “grace” is kept wherever English allows, so that the reader can see Paul presenting the Corinthians’ giving as an extension of God’s own generosity; only verse 16 has “thanks.”

verse.text: in a severe test of affliction, their overflowing joy and their deep poverty overflowed into the wealth of their generosity.
verse.note: The word’s basic sense is singleness or sincerity: an undivided, uncalculating disposition. In contexts of giving it shades into open-handedness, and most translators and lexicons accept “generosity” here. Some prefer “sincerity” or “single-mindedness,” which would make the point the Macedonians’ wholehearted motive more than the size of their gift.

verse.text: For they gave according to their means, I testify, and beyond their means, of their own accord,
verse.note: Verses 3–6 are a single loose sentence in Greek, and its first finite verb does not arrive until “they gave themselves” in verse 5. Most translations supply “they gave” here, as this one does. It is also possible to connect “of their own accord” directly with the giving of themselves in verse 5.

verse.text: begging us with much urging for the grace of sharing in the service to the holy ones—
verse.note: Paul uses this term for all believers as people set apart for God, echoing the Septuagint’s language for Israel; here it refers specifically to the believers in Jerusalem. “Saints” is retained by many translations, but now suggests canonized individuals or people of exceptional virtue. Other versions use “God’s people.”

The service in view is the collection of money Paul was organizing among his mostly Gentile assemblies for the poor believers in Jerusalem (see Romans 15:25–27; 1 Corinthians 16:1–4). The Greek word was an everyday term for carrying out a task on someone’s behalf, not for a religious office. Many translations have “ministry” or “relief” here. The phrase “sharing in” renders a word often translated “fellowship.”

verse.text: and this not merely as we had hoped, but they gave themselves first to the Lord and to us by the will of God,
so that we urged Titus that, just as he had already begun, so he should complete this grace too among you.
But just as you overflow in everything—in faith and speech and knowledge and all earnestness and the love from us that is in you—see that you overflow in this grace too.

note.term: the love from us that is in you

verse.note: The manuscripts are divided between “the love from us in you” and “the love from you in us” (that is, “your love for us”). The two differ by a swap of very similar pronouns. The reading translated here is the more difficult one and is adopted by the SBLGNT and other critical editions, but the choice is uncertain.

verse.text: I am not saying this as a command; rather, through the earnestness of others I am testing the genuineness of your love as well.
For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ: that for your sake he became poor, though he was rich, so that you by his poverty might become rich.
And in this matter I am giving my opinion, for this is to your advantage—you who already last year made a beginning not only in the doing but also in the wanting.
Now, then, complete the doing as well, so that just as there was eagerness in the wanting, so there may also be the completing, out of what you have.
For if the eagerness is there, it is acceptable according to whatever one has, not according to what one does not have.
For this is not so that others may have relief and you affliction, but as a matter of equality:
at the present time your surplus goes to their shortfall, so that their surplus may in turn go to your shortfall, so that there may be equality,
as it is written: “The one who gathered much did not have too much, and the one who gathered little did not have too little.”
verse.note: The quotation is from Exodus 16:18, about the manna in the wilderness: however much or little each Israelite gathered, each ended up with exactly enough. The Greek is compressed (“the one the much … the one the little”), and “gathered” is supplied from the Exodus context.

verse.text: But thanks be to God, who puts into the heart of Titus the same earnestness for you,
for he did accept our urging, but being more earnest still, he is setting out to you of his own accord.
verse.note: The Greek verbs here and in verses 18 and 22 (“we are sending”) are past tenses. Greek letter-writers regularly used the past tense from the reader’s point of view for actions accompanying the letter, and most scholars think Titus and the two brothers were carrying this letter to Corinth. If so, English needs a present tense. Read as ordinary past tenses, they would mean the party had already left before Paul wrote.

verse.text: With him we are sending the brother who is praised throughout all the assemblies for his work in the good news—
verse.note: The Greek word was an ordinary term for a public announcement of good news. “Gospel” is the traditional rendering, but it now sounds like a religious term or the title of a book. The Greek says literally “whose praise in the good news is through all the assemblies”; “for his work” is supplied, and whether that work was preaching or some other service to the message is not stated.

Paul names neither this brother nor the one in verse 22, presumably because the Corinthians would meet them when the letter arrived. Ancient and modern guesses include Luke and Barnabas, among others, but none can be confirmed.

verse.text: and not only that, but he has also been chosen by the assemblies as our traveling companion with this grace that is being administered by us, for the glory of the Lord himself and to show our eagerness—
we are guarding against this: that anyone should find fault with us over this large sum that is being administered by us,
for we take care to do what is honorable not only in the Lord’s sight but also in the sight of people.
And with them we are sending our brother, whom we have often tested and found earnest in many matters, and who is now much more earnest because of his great confidence in you.
As for Titus, he is my partner and fellow worker for you; as for our brothers, they are envoys of the assemblies, the glory of Christ.
verse.note: The Greek word is the one elsewhere translated “apostle.” Its ordinary meaning was someone sent with a commission, and here it describes delegates sent by the assemblies, not apostles in the sense of the Twelve or Paul. Most translations have “messengers” or “representatives”; “envoys” is used here to convey the element of official commissioning.

verse.text: So show them the proof of your love and of our boasting about you, in full view of the assemblies.
For about the service to the holy ones it is superfluous for me to write to you,
verse.note: The Greek word was an everyday term for service or for a task carried out on someone's behalf, not for a religious office. Here it refers to the collection Paul was organizing for the believers in Jerusalem. Most English versions use “ministry” for this word in church contexts and vary it elsewhere.

Paul uses this word for all believers as people set apart for God, echoing the Septuagint's language for Israel; here it means the community in Jerusalem. “Saints” now suggests canonized individuals or people of exceptional virtue. Many translations keep “saints”; others have “God's people.”

verse.text: for I know your eagerness, which I boast about on your behalf to the Macedonians, saying that Achaia has been ready since last year; and your zeal has stirred up most of them.
But I am sending the brothers so that our boast about you may not prove empty in this matter, so that you may be ready, just as I said you would be.
Otherwise, if Macedonians come with me and find you unprepared, we—to say nothing of you—would be put to shame in this undertaking.
verse.note: Most English versions render “in this confidence” or “for being so confident.” In the usage of the period the word normally names something objective, such as a plan or project one has taken on, and lexicographers have questioned whether the sense “confidence” is securely attested. The point is disputed, and the traditional rendering is still defended.

verse.text: So I considered it necessary to urge the brothers to go ahead to you and arrange ahead of time the bountiful gift you promised beforehand, so that it may be ready as a bountiful gift and not as something extorted.
verse.note: The Greek word is the ordinary word for “blessing,” which the Septuagint also uses for a generous present. Paul plays on it in verse 6, where “bountifully” is literally “on the basis of blessings.”

The word normally means greed. Here it may describe a gift wrung out of the Corinthians by pressure, as rendered, or a gift spoiled by their own grasping reluctance (“as one grudgingly given”). Translations are divided between the two.

verse.text: The point is this: whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and whoever sows bountifully will also reap bountifully.
Each of you should give as you have decided in your heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver.
verse.note: Paul echoes a line found in the Greek version of Proverbs 22:8 but not in the Hebrew text: “God blesses a cheerful and giving man.” He does not mark it as a quotation.

verse.text: And God is able to make all grace abound to you, so that in all things, at all times, you may have all you need and abound in every good work.
As it is written: “He scattered freely, he gave to the poor; his righteousness endures forever.”
verse.note: The quotation is Psalm 112:9 (111:9 in the Greek numbering), where “he” is the person who fears the Lord and gives generously. Greek has a single word-family where English has both “righteousness” and “justice”; here it means right conduct, shown in generosity to the poor. Some interpreters take Paul to be applying the line to God.

verse.text: Now he who supplies seed to the sower and bread for food will supply and multiply your seed and increase the harvest of your righteousness.
You will be enriched in every way for every kind of generosity, which through us produces thanksgiving to God.
verse.note: The word's basic meaning is singleness or sincerity, and in contexts of giving most translations take it as openhanded generosity, as here and in verse 13. Some lexicographers doubt that “generosity” is an established sense and prefer “sincere goodwill” or “wholeheartedness.”

verse.text: For the service of this public benefaction not only supplies what the holy ones lack but also abounds through many thanksgivings to God.
verse.note: Traditional versions render the phrase “the administration of this service” or “the ministry of this service.” In Greek cities the word named a public service that a citizen funded at personal expense; the Septuagint uses it for priestly service in the temple. Paul's readers may have heard either or both, and “public benefaction” follows the civic sense, which suits a collection of money.

verse.text: Through the proof that this service provides, they will glorify God for the obedience that goes with your confession of the good news of Christ and for the generosity of your sharing with them and with all,
verse.note: The Greek has a participle (“glorifying God”) with no stated subject. Most translations take it to be the believers in Jerusalem who receive the gift, as here; some take it to be the Corinthians (“you glorify God”).

The Greek was an ordinary word for a public announcement of good news, also used of imperial proclamations. “Gospel” has become a religious term or a book title. Many modern translations alternate between the two.

verse.text: and in their prayer for you they will long for you because of the surpassing grace of God upon you.
Thanks be to God for his indescribable gift!
verse.note: “Thanks” here is the same Greek word translated “grace” in verses 8 and 14. Paul plays on its range throughout his appeal for the collection: God's grace, the gracious gift, and the gratitude that returns to God. The “indescribable gift” is not specified; most take it to be Christ or God's grace given in him.

verse.text: Now I, Paul, appeal to you myself by the gentleness and forbearance of Christ—I who am lowly when face to face among you, but bold toward you when absent!
verse.note: The traditional pairing is “meekness and gentleness.” “Meek” now suggests weakness, which the first Greek word does not; “gentle” or “humble” is the mainstream modern rendering. The second word (epieikeia) describes someone with authority who does not insist on the full letter of their rights, so “forbearance” is used here; “clemency” or “kindness” are also defensible.

Paul is almost certainly echoing a taunt made against him in Corinth (compare verse 10): unimpressive and submissive in person, bold only from a distance. In ordinary Greek usage this word was often an insult, meaning low in status or servile, though Jewish and Christian writers also used it positively for humility. Paul repeats the jibe with irony.

verse.text: I beg you that when I am present I may not have to be bold with the confidence with which I count on daring to confront certain people who count us as walking according to the flesh.
verse.note: “Flesh” in Paul often means human nature left to its own resources and motives. To “walk according to the flesh” is to conduct oneself by merely human standards, which is the charge his critics made; in verse 3 he plays on the word, granting that he lives “in the flesh” as an ordinary mortal while denying that he fights by its methods.

verse.text: For though we walk in the flesh, we do not wage war according to the flesh.
For the weapons of our warfare are not weapons of the flesh but are powerful through God for tearing down strongholds. We tear down arguments
verse.note: The Greek is simply “powerful to God” or “powerful for God.” It may mean powerful by God’s agency, powerful in God’s service, or, as a Semitic-style intensive, “divinely powerful.” The rendering here follows the first reading, which is traditional, but the others are well supported.

verse.text: and every lofty obstacle raised up against the knowledge of God, and we take every thought captive into obedience to Christ,
and we stand ready to punish every disobedience, once your obedience is complete.
Look at what is in front of you. If anyone is confident of belonging to Christ, let that person consider once more that just as he belongs to Christ, so do we.

note.term: Look at what is in front of you.
note.traditional: Do ye look on things after the outward appearance?

verse.note: The Greek verb form can be a command (“Look at what is in front of you”), a statement (“You are looking only at appearances”), or a question (“Are you looking only at appearances?”). The command is chosen here because Paul normally uses this form as an imperative, but translations are divided. The phrase rendered “in front of you” is the same one translated “face to face” in verse 1.

verse.text: For even if I boast somewhat more about our authority, which the Lord gave for building you up and not for tearing you down, I will not be put to shame.
I do not want to seem as though I am trying to frighten you with my letters.
For someone says, “His letters are weighty and forceful, but his bodily presence is weak and his speech contemptible.”
verse.note: The Greek verb is singular, “he says.” It may refer to one particular critic at Corinth, which fits “such a person” in verse 11, or it may be used loosely in the manner of “people say” or “it is said.”

verse.text: Let such a person consider this: what we are in word by letter when absent, we are also in deed when present.

For we do not dare to class or compare ourselves with some of those who commend themselves. But they, measuring themselves by themselves and comparing themselves with themselves, show no understanding.
verse.note: A few manuscripts of the Western tradition lack the words “show no understanding. We, however,” at the end of verse 12 and the start of verse 13, so that it is Paul who measures himself by himself. The longer reading, translated here, is far better attested and is followed by nearly all modern editions.

verse.text: We, however, will not boast beyond measure, but according to the measure of the field that God allotted us as our measure—to reach even as far as you.
verse.note: The word (kanōn) basically means a measuring rod and so a rule or standard. Here and in verses 15–16 most modern interpreters take it to mean the area of work God assigned to Paul, hence “field,” “sphere” or “territory.” Others keep the sense “standard” or “limit.” The geographical language of reaching “as far as you” and “the regions beyond you” favors the former, but the matter is disputed.

verse.text: For we are not overextending ourselves, as though we did not reach you; we did come even as far as you with the good news of Christ.
verse.note: The traditional rendering is “gospel,” which is now a religious term or the name of a book. The Greek was an ordinary word for a public announcement of good news. Many modern translations alternate between “gospel” and “good news.”

verse.text: We do not boast beyond measure, in the labors of others, but we have hope that, as your faith grows, we will be greatly enlarged among you, in keeping with our field,

note.term: we will be greatly enlarged among you
note.traditional: we shall be enlarged by you

verse.note: The verb means to be made great or to be magnified. Paul may mean that his sphere of work will be widened with the Corinthians’ help, which fits the next verse, or that he will be held in greater honor among them. The Greek phrase rendered “among you” could also mean “by you.”

verse.text: so that we may bring the good news to the regions beyond you, and not boast in someone else’s field about work already done.
But “Let the one who boasts boast in the Lord.”

note.term: “Let the one who boasts boast in the Lord.”

verse.note: Paul gives no citation formula, but the words are a condensed form of Jeremiah 9:24 (9:23 in the Septuagint). He quotes the same line in 1 Corinthians 1:31, where he introduces it with “as it is written.”

verse.text: For it is not the one who commends himself who is approved, but the one whom the Lord commends.
I wish you would put up with a little foolishness from me. Yes, do put up with me!

note.term: Yes, do put up with me!

verse.note: The Greek verb form can be a command (“do put up with me”) or a statement (“but in fact you are putting up with me”). The command is the more common reading and is followed here; the statement is equally possible grammatically and is preferred by some interpreters.

verse.text: For I am jealous for you with God’s own jealousy, since I promised you in marriage to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ.
verse.note: Paul casts himself as the father of a bride, who arranged the betrothal and was responsible for his daughter’s faithfulness until the wedding. Betrothal was a binding commitment, so unfaithfulness in the interval counted as a betrayal of the husband. The picture echoes the prophets’ image of Israel as God’s bride.

verse.text: But I am afraid that, just as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, your minds may somehow be corrupted and turned from the sincerity and purity of your devotion to Christ.

note.traditional: the simplicity that is in Christ

verse.note: Some manuscripts lack the words “and purity”, and older translations based on them omit the phrase. Several of the earliest witnesses include it, and the edition translated here prints it, though scholars are not agreed on which form is original.

verse.text: For if someone comes and proclaims another Jesus whom we did not proclaim, or if you receive a different spirit that you did not receive, or different good news that you did not accept, you put up with it well enough.
verse.note: The Greek word was an ordinary term for the announcement of good news, used also of public and imperial proclamations. “Gospel” has become a purely religious term or a book title, so the plain meaning is given here, as many modern translations do in places. The related verb in verse 7 is rendered “announced the good news”.

verse.text: For I consider myself not in the least inferior to these super-apostles.
verse.note: Paul’s phrase is sarcastic, built on a rare adverb meaning “exceedingly”. It is disputed whether he means the rival missionaries in Corinth, whom he calls false apostles in verse 13, or the leading apostles in Jerusalem to whom those rivals may have appealed. The translation leaves the question open.

verse.text: Even if I am untrained in speaking, I am not untrained in knowledge; in every way we have made this plain to you in all things.
Or did I commit a sin by humbling myself so that you might be exalted, because I announced the good news of God to you free of charge?
I robbed other assemblies by taking pay from them so as to serve you,
verse.note: The Greek word meant a gathering of people, used both for a city’s civic assembly and, in the Greek Old Testament, for Israel gathered before God. “Church” is the near-universal rendering and is not wrong, but it now suggests a building or an institution. “Assembly” is used throughout this translation so the reader can see it is one word.

verse.text: and when I was with you and in need, I was a burden to no one, for the brothers who came from Macedonia supplied my need. In every way I kept myself from weighing on you, and I will keep doing so.
As the truth of Christ is in me, this boast of mine will not be silenced in the regions of Achaia.
Why? Because I do not love you? God knows I do.
But what I am doing I will keep on doing, to cut off the opening from those who want an opening, so that in what they boast about they may be found to be just as we are.
For such people are false apostles, deceitful workers, disguising themselves as apostles of Christ.
And no wonder, for Satan himself disguises himself as an angel of light.
So it is no great thing if his servants also disguise themselves as servants of righteousness. Their end will be according to their deeds.
I say again, let no one think me a fool. But if you do, then accept me even as a fool, so that I too may boast a little.
What I am saying I am not saying as the Lord would have it, but as in foolishness, in this undertaking of boasting.
verse.note: Most English versions render “in this boastful confidence”. In the Greek of the period the word normally names something objective, such as a plan or project one has taken on, and lexicographers have questioned whether the sense “confidence” is securely attested. The matter is disputed, and the traditional rendering remains defensible.

verse.text: Since many boast according to the flesh, I too will boast.
verse.note: “Flesh” here stands for merely human standards: ancestry, status and achievements of the kind listed in the verses that follow. It is set against speaking “as the Lord would have it” in the previous verse. Some translations paraphrase as “by human standards” or “as the world does”.

verse.text: For you gladly put up with fools, being so wise yourselves!
For you put up with it if someone enslaves you, if someone devours you, if someone takes advantage of you, if someone puts on airs, if someone strikes you in the face.
To my shame I say that we were too weak for that! But wherever anyone is daring—I am speaking in foolishness—I am daring too.
Are they Hebrews? So am I. Are they Israelites? So am I. Are they Abraham’s offspring? So am I.
Are they servants of Christ? I am talking like a madman—I am more so: in labors far more, in prisons far more, in beatings beyond measure, in danger of death many times.
Five times at the hands of Jews I received the forty lashes less one.
verse.note: This was a synagogue punishment. The Law of Moses limited a flogging to forty strokes (Deuteronomy 25:3), and Jewish practice stopped at thirty-nine to avoid exceeding the limit by a miscount. The beatings with rods in the next verse were, by contrast, a Roman punishment carried out by a magistrate’s attendants.

verse.text: Three times I was beaten with rods, once I was stoned, three times I was shipwrecked, a night and a day I have spent adrift on the deep;

on journeys many times, in dangers from rivers, dangers from bandits, dangers from my own people, dangers from Gentiles, dangers in the city, dangers in the wilderness, dangers at sea, dangers among false brothers;
verse.note: The Greek word names armed, violent plunderers such as highwaymen, as distinct from a thief who steals by stealth. “Robbers” is the usual rendering and is not wrong; “bandits” makes clearer the danger travelers faced on the roads.

The Greek word means “peoples” or “nations”; in Jewish usage the plural meant the non-Jewish peoples. This translation renders the same word “Gentiles” or “nations” according to sense. Here it is paired with “my own people”, meaning Paul’s fellow Jews.

verse.text: in labor and toil, often in sleepless nights, in hunger and thirst, often going without food, in cold and exposure.
Apart from everything else, there is the daily pressure on me: my anxiety for all the assemblies.

note.traditional: Beside those things that are without

verse.note: The Greek phrase can mean “apart from the things left unmentioned” or “apart from these external things”, that is, the outward hardships just listed. The first is the more common view today, and the rendering here is compatible with it. The word translated “pressure” may alternatively mean the daily stream of people or concerns coming at him.

verse.text: Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to stumble, and I do not burn?
verse.note: The verb means to trip someone up so that they fall in their loyalty to God, which is stronger than the modern sense of “offend”. Modern versions vary between “made to fall”, “made to stumble” and “led into sin”. “Burn” most likely means burning with indignation at whoever caused the fall, though some take it as burning with distress.

verse.text: If I must boast, I will boast of the things that show my weakness.
The God and Father of the Lord Jesus, he who is blessed forever, knows that I am not lying.
In Damascus the governor under King Aretas was guarding the city of the Damascenes in order to seize me,

note.traditional: the governor under Aretas the king

verse.note: Aretas IV was king of the Nabateans, an Arab kingdom with its capital at Petra, and ruled until about AD 40. The Greek title is “ethnarch”; whether this official governed Damascus for Aretas or was the head of the Nabatean community in the city is debated. Acts 9:23–25 tells of the same escape.

verse.text: and I was lowered in a basket through a window in the wall and escaped his hands.
I must boast. It does no good, but I will go on to visions and revelations of the Lord.

note.term: visions and revelations of the Lord

verse.note: The Greek genitive can mean visions and revelations given by the Lord or visions and revelations in which the Lord is seen. Most interpreters take it as the first, and some translations say “from the Lord.” The English “of the Lord” leaves both open, as the Greek does.

verse.text: I know a person in Christ who fourteen years ago—whether in the body I do not know, or out of the body I do not know; God knows—was snatched up to the third heaven.
verse.note: Paul is almost certainly describing his own experience in the third person, since verse 7 treats the revelations as his; the indirection lets him report it without boasting of it. The “third heaven” reflects Jewish pictures of the heavens as layered, numbered variously as three, five or seven. Here it is probably the highest, and the same place as the “paradise” of verse 4.

verse.text: And I know that such a person—whether in the body or apart from the body I do not know; God knows—
was snatched up into paradise and heard unutterable words, which no person is permitted to speak.
verse.note: The Greek adjective can mean either “impossible to put into words” or “not to be spoken,” the latter being a common term for sacred secrets. The clause that follows, about what no person is permitted to speak, favors the second sense. The Greek pairs “unspoken” with “spoken things,” a deliberate paradox that the English tries to keep.

verse.text: On behalf of such a person I will boast, but on my own behalf I will not boast, except in my weaknesses.
For if I should want to boast, I will not be a fool, for I will be speaking the truth. But I refrain, so that no one will credit me with more than what they see in me or hear from me,

even considering how extraordinary the revelations were. Therefore, so that I would not exalt myself, a thorn in the flesh was given to me, a messenger of Satan, to beat me, so that I would not exalt myself.

note.term: even considering how extraordinary the revelations were

verse.note: This phrase can close the sentence begun in verse 6, as here, or open the next one: “And because of the extraordinary revelations, so that I would not exalt myself…” Some manuscripts lack the word “therefore,” which makes the second reading easier. The edition translated here includes it, and so the phrase is attached to what precedes; translations are divided.

The word can mean a pointed stake, but in the Septuagint and in the ordinary Greek of the period it commonly means a thorn or splinter. What the affliction was is unknown; proposals include a chronic illness, a disability, and persecution or a particular opponent. “Messenger of Satan” could equally be translated “angel of Satan.”

verse.text: About this I pleaded with the Lord three times that it would leave me.
verse.note: “The Lord” here is most likely the risen Christ, since the reply speaks of “power” and Paul at once calls it “the power of Christ.” The reply in verse 9 is therefore marked as spoken by Jesus. A minority take “the Lord” as God the Father.

verse.text: And he has said to me, “My grace is enough for you, for power is brought to completion in weakness.” Most gladly, then, I will rather boast in my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may make its dwelling upon me.

note.term: power is brought to completion in weakness
note.traditional: my strength is made perfect in weakness

verse.note: The verb means to finish, carry through or bring to its goal; “made perfect” can suggest the removal of a flaw, which is not the point. Many manuscripts read “my power,” but the earliest lack “my,” and the edition translated here omits it. The sense is little changed, since the power in view is plainly the Lord’s.

verse.text: Therefore I am content with weaknesses, with insults, with hardships, with persecutions and distresses, for the sake of Christ; for whenever I am weak, then I am powerful.
I have become a fool; you forced me to it. For I ought to have been commended by you. For in nothing did I fall short of those super-apostles, even though I am nothing.
verse.note: The phrase is sarcastic, built on a rare adverb meaning “exceedingly, beyond measure.” Most scholars think it refers to the rival missionaries at Corinth whom Paul attacks in chapter 11. Others think it refers to the leading apostles in Jerusalem, whose authority those rivals claimed.

verse.text: The signs of an apostle were worked among you with all endurance, by signs and wonders and deeds of power.
verse.note: The Greek is the plural of the ordinary word for “power,” the same word used in verse 9, here meaning concrete acts that display it. “Miracles” is a fully acceptable rendering and is what most translations have. “Deeds of power” is used so that the link with “power” stays visible and the word stays distinct from “signs” and “wonders.”

verse.text: For in what were you made worse off than the rest of the assemblies, except that I myself was not a burden to you? Forgive me this injustice!
verse.note: The Greek word was the ordinary term for a civic gathering and the Septuagint’s word for Israel assembled before God. “Church” is the near-universal rendering and readers know what it refers to, but it now suggests a building or an institution. “Assembly” is used throughout this translation to keep the first-century sense in view.

verse.text: Look, for the third time now I am ready to come to you, and I will not be a burden; for I am not seeking what is yours, but you. For children are not obliged to save up for their parents, but parents for their children.
As for me, I will most gladly spend and be utterly spent for your souls. If I love you more, am I to be loved less?
But granted, I did not weigh you down; yet, crafty as I am, I caught you by deceit!

note.term: crafty as I am, I caught you by deceit

verse.note: Paul is not confessing but ironically voicing a charge made against him. The accusation seems to have been that he refused support in person only to profit through his envoys and the collection. The questions in verses 17 and 18 answer that charge.

verse.text: Did I take advantage of you through any of those I have sent to you?
I urged Titus to go, and I sent the brother with him. Titus did not take advantage of you, did he? Did we not walk in the same spirit? In the same footsteps?
Have you been thinking all along that we are defending ourselves to you? We are speaking before God in Christ. And all of it, beloved, is for building you up.

For I fear that when I come I may somehow find you not as I wish, and that I may be found by you not as you wish; that somehow there may be strife, jealousy, outbursts of anger, selfish ambition, slander, gossip, conceit, disorder.

I fear that when I come again my God may humble me before you, and I may mourn over many of those who sinned earlier and have not turned back from the impurity and sexual immorality and debauchery that they practiced.
